item.title: CoreWeave bond yields are approaching 19%. Why even stock investors should pay attention
item.description:
The AI infrastructure boom requires enormous amounts of capital

CoreWeave's falling bond prices offer a warning about the financial risks behind that expansion, even as demand for AI computing continues to grow.

Investors following CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) may want to look beyond its stock chart. On November 25, the yield on one of the company's bonds reached 17.91%, while another traded at a record-low price consistent with a yield of approximately 18.6%.

For shareholders, this is a development worth understanding as the stock is not too far from its all time low, apx 9% above its IPO opening price and still over 77% below its all time high

What are bonds, and why do their yields rise?

When a company issues a bond, it is essentially borrowing money from investors. In return, it promises to pay interest and repay the principal according to agreed terms.

Let's take CoreWeave's 9.75% bond, due in October 2031, as an example.

  • Face value: $1,000

  • Annual interest payments: $97.50

  • Market price on November 25: $742.30

  • Reported yield to maturity: 17.91%

Someone purchasing the bond at that price would pay $742.30 for a security scheduled to repay $1,000 at maturity, while also receiving interest payments along the way.

Assuming CoreWeave meets all its payment obligations, the discounted purchase price helps explain the considerably higher annualized yield.

But why would existing investors sell such a bond at a steep discount?

They may be concerned about the company's ability to repay its debt, require greater compensation for taking that risk, or prefer to reduce their exposure altogether.

When bond prices fall, their yields rise. An exceptionally high corporate bond yield is often a warning rather than a bargain.

CoreWeave is growing rapidly. So are its financing needs.

CoreWeave provides the computing infrastructure that companies use to develop and operate artificial intelligence applications. Building that infrastructure requires expensive chips, data centers, electricity and substantial upfront investment.

Its third-quarter financial results illustrate the financial challenge:

  • Quarterly revenue: $3.66 billion, up approximately 168% year over year.

  • Quarterly net interest expense: $846 million.

  • Quarterly net loss: $709 million.

  • Expected 2026 capital expenditure: $37 billion to $39 billion.

  • Expected fourth-quarter interest expense: $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion.

The company is generating considerably more revenue than a year ago. Yet financing its expansion remains expensive.

A company can experience tremendous demand for its products and still face financial difficulties if the cost of delivering those products and servicing its debt is too high.

Does CoreWeave now have to borrow at 18%?

Not necessarily.

The rising market yield does not automatically change the interest rate CoreWeave pays on its existing fixed-rate bonds. It does, however, suggest that raising new comparable unsecured debt could become considerably more expensive.

Consider a hypothetical company borrowing $1 billion at different interest rates:

The difference between borrowing at 7% and 18% would be $110 million in additional annual interest expenses.

Interestingly, Bloomberg reported on November 25 that CoreWeave's banks are preparing a $4.5 billion loan tied to its business with Meta Platforms. Preliminary pricing discussions reportedly center on 7%-7.5%, although the transaction has yet to be finalized.

The financing benefits from specific assets and a major customer contract, making its risk profile different from CoreWeave's unsecured corporate bonds.

This is a useful reminder that even a financially pressured company can have access to more attractive financing under certain conditions.

Why Nvidia and Nasdaq traders should care

CoreWeave is part of a much larger AI investment cycle.

Companies borrow money, purchase graphics processing units (GPUs), construct data centers and sell computing capacity to customers developing AI applications.

If financing becomes increasingly expensive across the industry, some companies may need to slow their expansion, postpone equipment purchases or raise additional equity from shareholders.

That could eventually affect chip manufacturers such as Nvidia (NVDA), data center operators and other businesses benefiting from AI infrastructure spending.

It does not mean that AI demand is disappearing. It raises a different question: how profitable and financially sustainable will meeting that demand be?

What stock traders should watch next

CoreWeave's bond prices could offer useful additional context when evaluating a recovery in its shares.

If CRWV stock rebounds while its bonds remain under considerable pressure, credit investors may still have reservations about the company's financial position.

A recovery in both the stock and bond prices would offer more encouraging evidence, particularly if accompanied by successful financing transactions.

The proposed Meta-related loan is another development worth following. Its final interest rate, size and investor demand could help reveal whether lenders are still comfortable financing substantial AI infrastructure projects when additional protections are available.

You don't need to trade bonds to benefit from watching them. The corporate bond market offers another perspective on the financial health of the companies whose shares you trade.

What else I'm watching: Is the stock market recovery gaining credibility?

While CoreWeave's bond market is sending a warning, other parts of the financial markets are showing early signs of improvement. The contrast is worth following.

Our latest investingLive earnings sentiment research shows that selling pressure following corporate earnings may be easing, particularly among larger companies. However, the recovery is still relatively narrow, with fewer than 40% of Wednesday's earnings reporters posting positive stock reactions.

There are encouraging developments overseas, too. As Justin Low reports, European stocks are rallying following Wall Street's remarkable turnaround. The bigger test will come next week, when US investors return from Thanksgiving and market liquidity normalizes.

Within the AI sector itself, my latest Nvidia stock analysis identifies several constructive technical developments. Nvidia has broken out of its descending channel and demonstrated some relative strength against Nasdaq futures. Reclaiming the $155 to $155.50 area would further strengthen its recovery case.

There is also an interesting historical perspective. As Eamonn Sheridan reports, Citi's research shows that the S&P 500 was higher six months later in 13 of the previous 14 instances when the VIX reached 40. Extreme fear has often presented opportunities for patient investors, although history offers no guarantees.

What I would particularly like to see is whether improving equity market sentiment is accompanied by an improvement in corporate bond prices.

If technology stocks continue recovering while the debt financing their expansion remains under severe pressure, I would treat the rally with some caution. A recovery in both markets would make a more convincing case that investors are regaining confidence in the AI investment cycle.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: EU leaders set to confirm backing for Spain's De Cos as next ECB President - report
item.description:
Reuters reports, citing EU diplomats, that EU leaders are set to sign off on Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next president of the European Central Bank.

This has been well telegraphed. Christine Lagarde is leaving early. She steps down on February 7, nine months before her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027. The timing is political. Leaving early lets EU leaders lock in a successor before April's French presidential election, where polls favour Marine Le Pen (and will be a major event in FX markets next year).

The race was really decided when Paris and Berlin agreed on a deal. France backed De Cos for the top job and proposed a Frenchwoman for the market operations role. That left Germany free to nominate the chief economist, and Berlin wants that seat for Princeton professor Markus Brunnermeier. The deal squeezed out Klaas Knot. Dutch media reported last week that he's expected to withdraw. The formal sign-off is aimed at the December 17-18 summit.

In terms of policy, De Cos was seen as slightly more dovish than Knot. More important is the backstop angle. He's a southern European and a Draghi ally, which reinforces the view that Frankfurt will step in if spreads blow out, whether that's true or not. T

There's nothing here for EUR/USD today. It's priced, and the ECB is a committee. Still, at the margin it's a mild dovish tilt and a vote for tighter BTP and OAT spreads into 2027. The next thing to watch is who gets the chief economist job. With Brunnermeier as the German pick, the hawks would keep a strong voice on the Executive Board and we're back to the typical dovish tilt at the ECB with the hawkish criticism coming from the Germans.

Today, the euro is up 14 pips to 1.0985.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: EUR/USD might be bottoming out amid peak Fed hawkishness and dovish repricing risks
item.description:
USD:

The US dollar has found support recently from a hawkish repricing in interest rate expectations following Governor Waller’s remarks, in which he even floated the possibility of a larger 50 bps hike at the December meeting. Higher-than-expected US inflation data added to the hawkish sentiment.

Moreover, the greenback benefited from safe-haven flows as global growth concerns intensified amid a more hawkish Fed, the prolonged US-Iran stalemate and a global stock market selloff.

Those same growth concerns, though, triggered a dovish repricing of Fed rate hike expectations further out the curve, as markets anticipated that the stock market rout could significantly weigh on the broader economy. This has caused the yield differential to favour the upside for the EUR/USD pair, although the greenback remained resilient thanks to safe-haven demand.

Looking ahead, we might see the US dollar coming under more pressure in case the Fed sounds less hawkish than expected or the economic data triggers a dovish repricing in interest rates expectations.

EUR:

On the EUR side, the ECB is widely expected to raise interest rates by 25 bps at the December meeting and deliver one final hike in June 2027. Growth is holding up well, but the recovery remains uneven, with France being a drag. Inflation and energy-related risks are still complicating the ECB’s job of getting inflation sustainably back to target.

France's 2027 budget battle is still ongoing, and the government is struggling to get its deficit-reduction plans through parliament. So, the French fiscal story remains unresolved. The key risk for French bonds is that parliament waters down the government's consolidation measures, leaving France with a higher deficit for longer. This could keep the French-German 10-year yield spread and the euro under pressure.

At the end of the day, the EUR/USD pair is 80% driven by what happens with the US dollar, so a dovish repricing in Fed interest rate expectations will likely outweigh euro-related woes, especially given the overbought US dollar positioning.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that EURUSDis consolidating near recent lows as traders await new catalysts. If we get a pullback into the downward trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into the 1.08 handle. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the major downward trendline around the 1.15 handle, with the 1.1270 level as the first target.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have a resistance zone around the 1.10 level. We can expect the sellers to step in around the resistance, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the downward trendline.

EURUSD TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor upward trendline defining the bullish momentum. The buyers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to pile in for a drop into new lows. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive European session wrap: European stocks ride Wall Street's comeback into Thanksgiving
item.description:
Headlines:

  • Heads up: Thanksgiving holiday leaves dip buyers in limbo
  • European stock market open: Stocks surge after stunning Wall Street turnaround
  • Gold remains caught between forced liquidations and hawkish Fed bets. What could trigger a reversal?
  • Crude oil finds some footing as prolonged US-Iran tensions keep the downside limited. What's next?
  • China hits back at Trump’s latest tariff threat as trade war tensions resurface
  • German consumer confidence remains in the doldrums heading into December
  • Month-end FX rebalancing signals favour the dollar - Credit Agricole
  • Bitcoin consolidates at yearly lows as traders await fresh catalyst amid negative backdrop

Markets:

  • AUD leads, CHF lags on the day
  • Gold down 0.3% to $3,571
  • European equities higher across the board
  • WTI crude oil up 1.0% to $84.51
  • Bitcoin up 1.0% to $60,796

There wasn't all too much in European trading today, with market players bracing themselves for a bit of a break in the second half of the week.

The Thanksgiving holiday is upon us and that will see US markets closed today before only opening for more of an abbreviated session tomorrow. As such, thinner liquidity conditions will be a key consideration and that means any modest order flows or sudden headlines could lead to exacerbated price movements in the days ahead.

But so far today, we are seeing a calmer mood in broader markets with European stocks catching a strong bounce after the Wall Street turnaround yesterday. Regional indices are holding gains well over 1% in erasing the more negative mood over the past few sessions, and even looking to post a weekly gain now. The DAX is up by 1.8% on the day with the CAC 40 up by 1.6% currently.

In the absence of US markets, the dollar is keeping calmer while showing little interest as the recent rally hits the pause button for a moment. EUR/USD is flat at 1.0974 with USD/JPY up by just 0.1% to 159.25 on the day.

As for the commodities space, we are seeing oil catch a little bounce with WTI crude up 1% to $84.51 while gold is struggling to build on yesterday's bounce and hold above $3,500 as the precious metal is down 0.3% to $3,571 today.

With the Thanksgiving holiday kicking into gear now, I'd be particularly wary of reading too much into any technical breakouts or breakdowns during the coming two days.

As much as the turnaround yesterday was quite encouraging, the real test for dip buyers will be whether they can continue to build on that momentum once the usual crowd returns next week. In the meantime, we'll have to deal with a quieter period with potential for some volatility bouts amid thinner liquidity conditions and also month-end flows perhaps.

For those enjoying the holidays, have a good break and I wish you a pleasant turkey day!

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Wall Street’s earnings mood is starting to improve. Is the stock market finding a bottom?
item.description:
Wall Street’s earnings mood is starting to improve. Is the stock market finding a bottom?

Exclusive investingLive research reveals early signs of recovery in post-earnings stock performance. Meanwhile, hedge funds have increased their short exposure, potentially setting the stage for a sharper rebound if market conditions stabilize.

November 26, 2026

Wall Street is showing signs that the selling pressure of recent weeks may be losing some of its effectiveness. Our latest earnings sentiment research, Wednesday's remarkable stock market recovery and the subsequent rally in European equities provide reasons for cautious optimism. But underneath the surface, plenty of stocks are still struggling.

investingLive Earnings Mood: 4.5 out of 10

Our proprietary earnings research shows an interesting discrepancy between how larger companies and the average stock are reacting to quarterly results.

Wednesday's average stock reaction, giving every company equal importance regardless of its size, was actually negative 4%

Deere gained approximately 4.4%, while HP jumped 11.5%. Excluding just these two companies would turn Wednesday's capitalization-weighted earnings reaction from positive 1.73% to negative 0.50%.

That is a fairly concentrated recovery.

Dell stock offers an encouraging clue

Dell Technologies (DELL) is one of the more interesting stocks to examine following Wednesday's trading session.

After reporting earnings on Tuesday evening, Dell fell more than 10% from its pre-earnings closing price before recovering the entire decline.

The initial selling was effectively rejected. For investors looking to identify a potential change in market sentiment, these failed selloffs can be particularly informative.

Dick's Sporting Goods and Abercrombie & Fitch also extended their initial earnings gains, bringing their cumulative advances to approximately 18.6% and 26%, respectively.

There are less encouraging examples, of course. Nutanix, Ambarella and Urban Outfitters suffered double-digit earnings declines.

Nasdaq and S&P 500 futures are showing early signs of stabilization

Wednesday's selloff presented bears with an opportunity to establish fresh lows below those recorded last Friday. Neither of the two major equity futures markets did so.

Both markets have recovered approximately 5% from their November 20 lows.

For traders, two upside references are particularly interesting:

  • Nasdaq futures: 27,137, Monday's high.
  • S&P 500 futures: 7,313.25, Monday's high.

Reclaiming and sustaining prices above these levels would strengthen the recovery case. Conversely, breaking last Friday's lows would undermine it considerably.

European markets are also participating in the relief rally, with the Euro Stoxx gaining 1.8% and Germany's DAX rising 1.6% at Thursday's opening, as Justin Low reported in his European stock market update.

Hedge funds are positioned for trouble. Could that help the bulls?

According to Goldman Sachs, hedge fund clients reduced their exposure for five consecutive weeks before aggressively increasing their short positions.

As Eamonn Sheridan reported, ETF short exposure recorded its third-largest weekly increase in a decade.

Such positioning creates an interesting possibility. If stocks continue stabilizing, some short sellers may begin buying back shares to close their positions, while other fund managers may gradually increase their market exposure.

That could accelerate a recovery. It does not necessarily require a major improvement in corporate fundamentals to get started, although sustained gains would need broader support.

Nvidia remains central to the recovery

Earlier today, our Nvidia stock analysis identified several encouraging technical developments, including its rebound from $141.17 and a break above its descending price channel.

The fundamental picture is more complicated.

S&P has placed Nvidia’s AA credit rating on negative watch, while Moody’s has maintained its Aa1 rating and stable outlook. Both have raised concerns surrounding governance and dependence on Jensen Huang.

Nvidia's ability to sustain its recovery despite these lingering concerns could provide another indication of whether investors are becoming more comfortable taking risk again.

What stock market investors should watch next

Three developments would make the bullish case more convincing:

  • More companies attracting buyers after earnings, rather than a handful of influential stocks supporting the averages.
  • Recent earnings winners retaining their gains and more initial selloffs reversing, as Dell's did.
  • Nasdaq and S&P 500 futures establishing higher highs and higher lows.

With US stock exchanges closed for Thanksgiving and reopening for a shortened Friday session, next week should provide a better test of conviction.

There is enough evidence to start questioning the bearish narrative. There is not yet enough to declare that the correction is over.

Educational market analysis by investingLive.com. Invest and trade at your own risk.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Connecting the dots: Is big tech starting to outgrow its own valuation playbook?
item.description:
One of the things that Wall Street has always loved about big tech is its ability to make an obscene amount of money without having to spend an equally obscene amount of money to grow. Or at least that used to be how it used to be.

Historically, the appeal of software and digital platforms has always been their ability to scale. Selling another million software subscriptions doesn't necessarily require building another factory. As such, revenues can grow much faster than the cost of doing business. And that is part of the reason Wall Street has been so comfortable attaching lofty valuations to tech stocks. However, the AI trade is a completely different beast.

Between the need for data centres, expensive chips, electricity and networking infrastructure, growth is becoming a much more expensive affair.

And as investors are grappling with the latest selloff in tech stocks, perhaps we should be asking how big of an issue is the changing economics of the tech business itself? Let's try to put things into perspective.

According to a research published by Brookings, the combined capex by Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle is projected to exceed $800 billion this year. For some context, that figure was just a measly $97 billion back in 2020.

And what is even more striking is that their combined capital spending is projected to exceed the cash generated by their operations.

In July, an analysis by Reuters suggested that for every additional dollar of operating cash flow that these companies are expected to generate between 2025 and 2027, they will be increasing capital spending by roughly $1.57.

In simpler terms, it means that as the businesses grow, then so is the cost of delivering that growth.

So, what exactly does all of this mean for valuations?

Well, just imagine two companies generating $100 billion in operating cash flow. One needs to reinvest $20 billion, while the other needs to reinvest $80 billion. Would you be comfortable paying the same price for both, assuming that they hold similar future growth prospects? Bzzt. I certainly wouldn't.

And that's the point that investors seem to be waking up to in the last few months. If we're still valuing tech stocks primarily on revenue and earnings growth, we risk overlooking how much more expensive that growth is becoming. Capital spending takes a bite out of cash flow upfront, while depreciation will weigh on reported earnings for years to come.

To put things into a simpler question: Does a tech company growing its earnings by 20% today deserve the same valuation multiple as it did five years ago if it now needs to commit considerably more capital to deliver that same growth?

For me, that's where the traditional valuation playbook might need a bit of a rethink. Or perhaps we're already seeing that change in the way that investors have been reacting to even some of the blockbuster earnings beats on Wall Street as of late.

It used to be that beating earnings estimates and raising revenue guidance was pretty much the dream combination for tech stocks. These days, investors also want to know how much bigger the cheque is going to be to deliver on those promises.

As such, I reckon that free cash flow yields and returns on invested capital are going to feature much more prominently in the conversation going forward. In looking at the next phase, it might not necessarily be the fastest-growing tech companies that deserve the richest valuations anymore. Instead, it is those that can turn that growth into meaningful returns without constantly having to reach deeper into their pockets.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: What really drives the FX market? A look at interest rate differentials
item.description:
The FX market is highly sensitive to interest rates. This is one of the most important concepts to understand when trading currencies. In fact, interest rate differentials are the main drivers of major currencies.

 The reason for this relationship is pretty simple: higher interest rates tend to attract foreign investment, increasing the demand and value of the currency. On the other hand, lower interest rates tend to be less attractive for foreign investment and decrease the currency's value. Therefore, monetary policy divergence (or better yet divergence in interest rate expectations) between two countries is the key driver.

 

Emerging market currencies are generally driven by changes in the US dollar and certain commodities due to the impact they have on their economies and the perceived risk from investors. You are unlikely to be trading those since they have wider spreads, higher costs, increased risks and generally have limited availability with retail brokers.

 

Now, imagine that US interest rates are significantly higher than euro-area interest rates. An investor deciding where to allocate capital may find US assets more attractive because they offer a higher yield. To purchase those US assets, the investor generally needs US dollars. This creates demand for USD. This is one reason why interest-rate differentials are so important in FX.

 

Suppose the Federal Reserve is expected to keep interest rates at 5%, while the European Central Bank is expected to reduce rates toward 2%. If those expectations become stronger, the yield advantage of US assets over European assets increases. All else being equal, this will increase demand for the dollar and place downward pressure on EUR/USD.

 

This is where the relationship between the bond market and FX market becomes important. Bond yields provide a direct way of observing market expectations for interest rates, inflation and economic growth. FX traders therefore often monitor government bond yields and interest-rate differentials when analysing currencies.

 

FX and Yield Differentials

 

Currencies are traded in pairs, so in order to visually see the relationship between interest rates and currencies you need to take the difference between the respective country’s bond yields (interest rates) and the corresponding FX pair. To simplify things, think about bond yields as interest rates.

 

Let’s see an example with EUR/USD. Since you have the EUR as the base currency, you need to take the yield on the German bond (which is used as benchmark for the Eurozone economy) and since you have the USD as the quote currency, you take the US bond yield. The difference between the yield on the German bond and the US one gives you the yield spread or yield differential. We will use the 2-year yield because it’s more sensitive to near-term changes in central bank monetary policy expectations.

Now if we compare the yield spread (black line) with the EUR/USD price chart (blue line), you can clearly see the tight correlation in the chart above. You can check yourself with any other major currency pair and the respective 2-year yield spread, if you want more proof.

 

 

Keep in mind that sometimes the FX pair can diverge with yield spreads. There can be many reasons in the short-term affecting the currency pair but eventually the exchange rate generally catches up with the yield spread.

 

For example, the last divergence in 2018/2019 was caused by weakening growth in the Eurozone and global risk aversion due to the US-China trade war. Even if the Fed started to cut interest rates in 2019, the US dollar benefited from safe haven flows.

 

The divergences tell you that you shouldn’t trade just based on the charts and correlations but look for reasons and keep yourself informed on the latest developments to give you a better edge. When you start to see a divergence, it could be a signal that the market is getting overstretched, so you can prepare to strike as soon as the picture changes and you get the right catalysts.

 

That’s why knowing what’s priced in is critical. The pricing and repricing in interest rate expectations is what moves the major currencies the most.

Despite interest rates expectations being the main drivers of major currencies, they are not the only factor. FX markets are also influenced by economic growth, inflation, risk sentiment, and geopolitical developments.

Other Factors Influencing the FX Market

 

Economic growth matters because stronger economies tend to provide better investment opportunities and can influence expectations for future interest rates. Suppose US economic growth consistently exceeds expectations while European growth deteriorates. Traders may expect the Fed to maintain tighter monetary policy while the ECB becomes more likely to cut rates. This combination can create both a growth and interest-rate advantage for the US, supporting the dollar.

Inflation is equally important because central banks respond to inflation when determining monetary policy. If inflation unexpectedly accelerates, markets may begin pricing higher interest rates. This can cause short-term bond yields to rise and support the currency. For example, if US inflation comes in significantly above expectations, traders may conclude that the Federal Reserve will have less room to cut rates. US Treasury yields may rise, and the dollar could strengthen as markets reprice the expected path of US monetary policy.

 

The opposite can happen with weaker inflation. If inflation falls faster than expected, markets may begin pricing earlier or more aggressive rate cuts. Treasury yields may decline and the dollar may weaken. You can see that eventually everything comes down to changes in expectations for future interest rates. 

 

Remember that themarket reacts to changes in expectations, not simply to economic data or events in isolation. A strong economic number does not automatically mean the currency will rise. What matters is whether the number will change expectations about future central bank action compared to what’s already priced in. 

 

Central banks are therefore among the most important participants to monitor. Markets are forward-looking. A central bank does not need to change interest rates for the currency to move. If its communication changes expectations about future policy, the FX market can react immediately.

 

For example, suppose the Federal Reserve leaves rates unchanged but signals that it expects to cut rates several times over the following year. Even though the current policy rate has not changed, markets may immediately price lower future rates. Treasury yields can fall and the dollar can weaken.

 

Risk Sentiment

Another important factor in FX is risk sentiment. Some currencies tend to behave differently depending on whether investors are comfortable taking risk. The Japanese yen and Swiss franc, for example, are often associated with defensive or "safe-haven" demand, while currencies such as the Australian dollar can be more sensitive to global growth and risk appetite.

 

During periods of market stress, investors may reduce exposure to riskier assets and increase demand for perceived safe-haven assets. This can produce large moves in currencies even when there has been no major change in domestic economic fundamentals.

 

For example, imagine a sudden geopolitical crisis causes investors to become extremely risk averse. Equity markets sell off and volatility increases. The most famous safe haven in the FX space is the Swiss Franc (CHF), although the US dollar and the Japanese yen have also safe haven characteristics. 

 

Conclusion

To sum up, you have to think about the currencies as two economies being in competition with each other. When looking at EUR/USD, for example, you are effectively comparing the economic and monetary policy outlook of the United States versus the Eurozone.

 

You are trying to determine which side of the currency pair has the stronger probability of outperforming the other based on interest rates expectations which are ultimately influenced by growth, inflation and the central bank. 

 

The goal is to understand why capital should move from one currency into another, what is causing investors to change their expectations, and whether the market has already priced that information in.

This is THE most important lesson you will ever learn about the FX market. If you master this, you will become a very good FX trader. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Zcash continues to face macro headwinds despite improving adoption developments. What's next?
item.description:
Zcash continues to face a challenging macro environment, much like the broader crypto market, as tightening financial conditions, hawkish Fed and risk-off flows continue to weigh on risk appetite. Keep in mind that higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions are a headwind for risk assets, especially cryptocurrencies, which are sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk appetite.

Looking at Zcash-specific news, we have the ongoing governance debate over Zcash's development funding. Coinholders are voting until November 30 on a proposal to remove 50,000 ZEC (roughly $50 million at the time of the proposal) from the Community Grants treasury and redirect future funding towards a development and legal-defence fund. item.title: Macro pulse: Is the Santa Claus rally losing its magic on Wall Street?
item.description:
The trouble with market traditions is that we sometimes forget to ask whether they still work.

With December just around the corner, you can expect to hear plenty of chatter about the Santa Claus rally coming to town in the weeks ahead. And after the rather miserable November we've had in Wall Street, investors will be surely hoping for a bit more of a Christmas cheer to wrap up the year.

But before we get too carried away with the festive spirit, let's revisit the whole concept of the Santa Claus rally. The thing that we should really be asking is whether it is still as useful a seasonal trading tool as it once was.

For those unfamiliar with the phenomenon, it typically refers to the tendency for US stocks to rise during the final five trading days of December and the first two of January. And there's good reason why it has earned a place in Wall Street's trading calendar.

According to LPL Research, the S&P 500 has historically averaged a gain of 1.3% during this window as compared to just 0.3% during a typical seven-day trading period.

Taken at face value, there is certainly the temptation to trade on those numbers alone. However, let's take a step back and remind ourselves that markets of today definitely do not behave like markets of yesteryear. After all, that research figure is one that dates back to 1950. Talk about the stone age for markets, eh?

And when we break down the numbers a little further, we get a rather different picture.

While the average return during the Santa Claus rally stretches to 1.25% going back to 1950, that figure drops to 0.80% since 2001 and just 0.48% over the past decade.

And when viewing the frequency of positive returns, that hasn't diminished nearly as much. Even over the past ten years, the S&P 500 has still posted gains on seven occasions. So, perhaps it's not so much that Santa has stopped showing up on Wall Street. It is just that he has been a little less generous with his presents.

Having said all that, I do wonder just how much of the seasonal advantage might have been eroded by the popularity of the trade itself. It's kind of like the January seasonal gold trade, which sometimes now have turned into frontrunning in December.

In this case, if everyone knows that stocks tend to go up during the final few trading days of the year, then what's stopping investors from getting a head start on their Christmas shopping?

Looking to December this year though, there's certainly no shortage of things that could spoil the festive mood. Stubborn inflation pressures, the prospects of further tightening by the Fed, and growing scrutiny over AI valuations all make for a rather troubling backdrop.

As such, I would feel much more comfortable in seeing a broadening recovery in equities alongside some reprieve in the bond market than by what the seasonal calendar has to say.

Don't get me wrong. I still think there's value in paying attention to seasonality when it comes to trading. However, we have to be mindful that markets evolve and what might have been a rewarding trade a couple of decades ago may not offer quite the same windfall today.

As much as one believes in the Santa Claus rally, it is always best to also be reminded that seasonal pattenrs should help line your pockets in building your overall market view. It should not be the one to dictate it.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Month-end FX rebalancing signals favour the dollar - Credit Agricole
item.description:
As if the dollar needed another excuse to stay bid this month. As November trading draws toward a close, we're getting to that time of the month when portfolio rebalancing flows can throw a little spanner in the works for FX traders.

This time around, Credit Agricole's month-end fixing model is pointing to moderate dollar buying across the board, with the strongest buy signal coming against the Swedish krona. The firm notes that:

"Global equity markets were lower across the board in November. In FX, the USD has outperformed across the board on the month. Overall, the moves in equity markets, when adjusted for market capitalisation and FX performance this month, suggest month-end portfolio-rebalancing flows are likely to be moderate USD buying across the board with the strongest buy signal in the case of the USD vs SEK."

For the uninitiated, think of these flows as a bit of housekeeping being done by large fund managers. As the value of their investments changes throughout the month, they may need to buy or sell currencies to bring their portfolio allocations and currency hedges back in line by the end of it.

As such, these flows aren't necessarily a reflection of what the general market backdrop or conviction is playing out to be.

The added complication for November though is that there is also the Thanksgiving holiday thinning out liquidity today and tomorrow. While the month-end fixing on Monday next week will be one to watch, any sizeable orders coming through before then could also have an outsized impact if liquidity conditions remain subdued as that could lead to exacerbated price movements. So, just be wary of that as well over the next two days.

As a reminder, do remember that these flows should not be treated as a hard directional call. They are notoriously difficult to pin down and tend to take on more importance as we get closer to the fix itself. If anything else, think of them as another piece of the puzzle rather than the main driver of price action.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

The bigger test will only come next week when US investors return and we get a better sense of whether there is any conviction behind the latest rebound. In essence, dip buyers have bought themselves some breathing room. Now, can they make it count?

item.title: China hits back at Trump’s latest tariff threat as trade war tensions resurface
item.description:
It looks like a trade war is back on the menu again. Just when markets thought they could afford to spend a little less time worrying about US-China tensions, we're back to the familiar exchange of threats between Washington and Beijing this week.

China's commerce ministry is hitting back at the latest US tariff proposals today, expressing firm opposition to Washington's Section 301 investigation into structural overcapacity.

"China urges the US to correct its erroneous practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation. China will closely monitor developments and reserves the right to take necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests."

As a reminder, the US is proposing additional tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners and that includes a 20% tariff on Chinese goods. In doing so, the latest proposal would bring the average effective tariff rate on Chinese goods back up to roughly 31%.

In essence, US president Trump is looking to rebuild his tariffs wall after the Supreme Court struck down earlier levies.

Now, the language from Beijing is a familiar one and something that we have seen a lot of in the past. At the end of the day, there is a difference between threatening retaliation and actually delivering it. On the latter, I'd actually pay more attention on how Beijing might look to hit back through other avenues. To put it more simply, I'm more interested as to when they will start to bring rare earth export restrictions back into the conversation.

As for markets, the timing of all this is hardly ideal. Investors are already wrestling with a rather painful tech selloff and renewed concerns about economic growth. So when you throw in another round of tariffs uncertainty into the mix, it definitely complicates the recovery effort.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Chart of the day: Swiss franc emerges as a quiet winner in the market turmoil
item.description:
Amid all the selling in equities this week, the Swiss franc is quietly emerging as one of the more notable winners in the major currencies space. And considering how other traditional safe havens have been behaving lately, it's not all too surprising to see the appeal of the franc.

Gold is struggling to keep its head above water, while the Japanese yen remains weighed down by fiscal worries and uncertainty surrounding the BOJ policy outlook. So if you're a trader looking to put your money somewhere safe without necessarily piling into the dollar, the franc makes for a rather compelling alternative.

In that regard, EUR/CHF is arguably one of the more interesting charts to watch among major currencies this week. The pair briefly breached below the 0.9100 mark yesterday, taking it to its lowest levels since March. All that before finding some respite from the late turnaround in Wall Street and then keeping steadier today just above the figure level.

That being said, the technical picture isn't exactly encouraging for buyers at the moment. The November recovery stalled around 0.9255-75, with sellers subsequently taking out both the 0.9200 level and the previous swing region around 0.9175.

Right now, it's all on a test of the May lows near the 0.9100 level. A sustained break below that could open the door for a revisit of the March lows near 0.9000.

As for buyers, there is work to do in first needing to get back above the early November lows around 0.9130-35 to start. After which, a push back above 0.9200 would be needed to regain more conviction in search of a stronger rebound.

Putting the technicals aside for a bit, let's not forget about the fact that the SNB won't necessarily be thrilled about a stronger franc. That is especially the case given Switzerland's inflation backdrop, or should I say lack thereof. So, that's a policy risk worth keeping in the back of one's mind.

But for now, I would argue that EUR/CHF is acting as a useful barometer of broader market anxiety. If traders continue to run for cover and gold and the yen aren't offering much shelter, then the franc could find itself with plenty more admirers in the near-term.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: German consumer confidence remains in the doldrums heading into December
item.description:

German consumer sentiment edged up heading into December but continues to remain subdued as a whole, according to the latest GfK/NIM survey.

The breakdown shows that economic expectations falling to -1.6 from 2.1 while price expectations also nudged up a little to 2.8 from 1.0 previously. THe only real bright spot is that income expectations improved a little to -13.9 from -15.7 before this. But at the balance, the report is still suggesting that consumer confidence remains in the dumps.

GfK/NIM even noted that the index was "more or less stagnating at a low level" and that doesn't bode well ahead of the Christmas shopping season.

If anything else, this does provide some suggestion to the ECB that the euro area's largest economy is still not exactly recovering all too well despite the more resilient showing in the first half of the year. The second half of the year looks to be one of consolidating and stagnating momentum, which isn't the most ideal situation as inflation pressures remain strong.

For now, policymakers may still get away with another rate hike, or perhaps even two, but the challenge will grow to be greater next year amid higher stagflationary risks potentially.

item.title: BOJ policymaker Tamura hints at faster rate hikes, keeps December in focus
item.description:
A 50 bps rate hike by the BOJ? Now, wouldn't that be something?

We're hearing more comments from BOJ policymaker Tamura today and he is not shying away about talking up the prospect of more aggressive rate hikes by the central bank. His latest remarks:

  • I do have an image in mind of raising interest rates once every few months
  • If inflation risks materialise, BOJ may need to speed up pace of rate hikes or even deliver a 50 bps rate hike
  • Stock, asset price moves are among factors we will look at in measuring financial conditions
  • Would look to decide policy by looking at the data, as well as economic, financial developments leading up to December meeting

Before we get too carried away by the headlines though, let's remember who we're dealing with here. Tamura has been one of the leading hawks at the BOJ since joining the central bank in July 2022. So, none of this is particularly out of character.

As such, the more interesting question is whether how other policymakers are feeling and if they are viewing things the same way as Tamura is. For now, there's no real suggestion of any overly hawkish leanings along the same lines at least.

For the most part, the BOJ has already acknowledged that underlying inflation has broadly reached its 2% target. However, they're not explicitly taking any steps or setting out a position to pre-commit to a rate hike for December and also for next year.

As things stand, traders are pricing in roughly 70% odds of a 25 bps rate hike in December. While the odds are solid, they're not exactly screaming conviction just yet. And I doubt Tamura's remarks alone will do much to move the needle on that front.

What would carry more weight is if we start hearing a similar sense of urgency from some of the less hawkish members of the BOJ. That's where I'd be looking for clues in the run-up to the December meeting.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Asia stocks extend rebound
item.description:
• My Nvidia stock analysis shows bulls are better than what most seem to think
  • Ray Dalio's 10-15% gold call resurfaces as bullion tries to find its feet
  • Franklin Templeton adds Hyperliquid's HYPE to its EZPZ crypto index ETF from December 1
  • Bank of Korea signals more hikes as 15 of 21 rate projections sit above 3.25%
  • S&P puts Nvidia's AA rating on watch for a possible cut, as Moody's holds steady
  • Goldman says hedge funds pile into shorts, with ETF shorts posting a 19-point weekly jump
  • PBOC sets USD/ CNY reference rate for today at 6.7096 (vs. estimate at 6.6655)
  • BoJ's Tamura says rates must reach neutral 'soon', still sees neutral near 2%
  • Bank of Korea hikes to 3.25%, sees 4.1% growth in 2027 as chip boom drives economy
  • The RBA's three 'stars' are fuzzier than they look: what it means for AUD and stocks
  • Australia's data centre boom drives the biggest capex jump in years, near mining-boom highs
  • Nikkei and Kospi rebound over 1% as Asia follows Wall Street's comeback, BoK decision next
  • Citi says fear is extreme, but stocks rose after 13 of 14 past VIX spikes to 40
  • Projectile explodes near tanker 50 nautical miles off Dubai as Gulf shipping attacks mount
  • From Tokyo suburbs to the Australian outback, data centre pushback is a growing AI risk
  • Michael Burry closes his Nasdaq bets and shifts to value, but still plans an Nvidia short
  • BofA sees S&P 500 at 7,800 by end-2027, a target that only takes it back to October
  • AI's debt binge is becoming a bond market problem, South Africa's central bank warns
  • Moody's keeps Nvidia at Aa1 after Huang's return but flags key-person and governance risks
  • Gold claws back $160 from a 14-month low, but one candle doesn't necessarily make a bottom
  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 25 Nov: It’s a Wrap. S&P 500 and Nasdaq pare steep losses
  • A junk-rated borrower with an AA-rated customer: CoreWeave's next loan leans on Meta

Summary:

  • Stocks: the Nikkei rose about 1.6%, the Kospi about 1.5% and the Hang Seng about 1.9%, led by chipmakers, while Shanghai was flat
  • US futures: S&P 500 futures gained about 0.7% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 1.1%, with Wall Street closed for Thanksgiving
  • Bank of Korea: it hiked to 3.25% with two dissents, and 15 of 21 board projections sit above 3.25%
  • BoJ: Tamura said rates should reach a neutral level of around 2% "soon", and Japanese 2-year yields rose about 4bp
  • Australia: capex jumped 12.2% against a 4.4% forecast, and AUD/USD rose to around 0.6646
  • Nvidia ratings: S&P put Nvidia's AA rating on CreditWatch negative, while Moody's held at Aa1
  • Gold: it steadied near $3,590 and Brent traded near $91 after a tanker incident off Dubai

Asian stocks extended their recovery on Thursday, led by chipmakers, as two of the region's central banks struck hawkish tones and US stock futures rose in thin trade with Wall Street closed for Thanksgiving.

Equities: chips lead a second day of gains

Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 1.6% to around 57,900, adding to its early gains, while the broader Topix rose about 0.5%. South Korea's Kospi climbed about 1.5% and the tech-heavy Kosdaq more than 2%, as SK Hynix gained about 3.5% and Samsung Electronics about 1.7%. The moves recovered part of Wednesday's heavy losses, when the Kospi fell more than 6%.

In China, Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose about 1.9%, while the Shanghai Composite was little changed. US stock index futures built on Wall Street's late rebound on Wednesday, with S&P 500 futures up about 0.7% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 1.1% higher.

Central banks: Seoul hikes, Tokyo hawk pushes

The Bank of Korea raised its base rate by a quarter point to 3.25%, its third hike since July, as expected. The decision drew two dissents, from board members Lee Soo-hyung and Hwang Kun-il, but the board's projections leaned hawkish: 15 of 21 put the rate above 3.25% in six months, including seven at 3.75%. The bank said inflation will stay above target for a prolonged period and that the timing of further hikes will depend on inflation, growth and financial stability. It forecast growth of 3.9% this year and 4.1% in 2027, driven by semiconductor exports.

In Japan, Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura said the policy rate should be brought to neutral "soon", repeating his view that neutral is around 2%, well above the current 1.25%. He said the BoJ should "make haste slowly" but be ready to speed up hikes if inflation overshoots. Japanese two-year government bond yields rose about 4 basis points to around 1.76%, while the 10-year yield edged up to around 2.66%. The yen barely moved, with USD/JPY holding near 159.10.

Australia: capex surges

Australian private capital spending jumped 12.2% in the third quarter, almost three times the 4.4% forecast, as equipment investment surged 23.1% to a record, led by the industry that includes data centres. Firms also lifted their spending plans for 2026-27 by 11.8% to about A$224 billion. The Australian dollar rose about 0.3% to around 0.6646.

AI and credit: the stress shifts to governance and funding

S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's AA rating on CreditWatch negative, warning of a possible one-notch downgrade within 90 days over concerns about board independence, key-person risk and export-control questions. Moody's, by contrast, kept its Aa1 rating and stable outlook. Elsewhere, CoreWeave's banks are preparing a $4.5 billion loan backed by a Meta contract, even as the cost of insuring CoreWeave's own debt hit a record. South Africa's central bank warned that AI firms now compete with governments for long-term funding. Resistance to data centre projects is spreading too, from Tokyo's suburbs to Australia's Northern Territory and across the United States.

Sentiment calls were mixed. Citi Wealth said extreme investor fear offers a buying opportunity, Bank of America set a cautious S&P 500 target of 7,800 for the end of 2027, and Goldman Sachs said hedge funds have been adding short positions. Michael Burry closed his remaining bearish bets on the Nasdaq-100 but said he still plans to short Nvidia nearer $200.

Commodities: gold steadies, oil holds gains

Gold held near $3,590 an ounce after Wednesday's sharp reversal from a 14-month low near $3,425, while Ray Dalio's recommendation of a 10% to 15% gold allocation drew renewed attention. Silver rose about 1.2%. Brent crude traded around $91 a barrel after a tanker reported a nearby explosion from an unknown projectile 50 nautical miles west of Dubai late on Wednesday, the latest in a string of attacks on Gulf shipping. Bitcoin rose about 3% to around $61,000.

Ahead

US stock and bond markets are closed for Thanksgiving, and Friday is a shortened session. Thin liquidity may keep moves exaggerated into the weekend. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Heads up: Thanksgiving holiday leaves dip buyers in limbo
item.description:
The turkey couldn't have come at a more awkward time for Wall Street, could it?

Just as things were starting to get interesting again after yesterday's impressive recovery, US traders are now off to enjoy their Thanksgiving break.

As a reminder, US stock and bond markets will be closed today in observance of Thanksgiving. And even though trading resumes tomorrow, Wall Street will only be open until 1800 GMT (1pm ET) while the bond market will wrap things up at 1900 GMT (2pm ET).

But in reality, many market participants will already have one foot out the door until Monday. So, one can reasonably expect thinner liquidity conditions across broader markets over the next two days - especially during US trading hours.

That being said, let's not mistake a lack of liquidity for a lack of volatility.

With fewer buyers and sellers around, it takes considerably less money to move markets. Any relatively modest order size or unexpected headlines could make for some rather exaggerated moves in currencies, gold and stock futures.

And given how fragile the market sentiment is looking this week, I'd be particularly wary of reading too much into any technical breakouts or breakdowns during the coming two days.

As much as the turnaround yesterday was quite encouraging, the real test for dip buyers will be whether they can continue to build on that momentum once the usual crowd returns next week. All eyes will be on tech stocks to see if they can sustain a more meaningful recovery from here, or is this just another half-hearted attempt at buying the dip like we saw on Monday?

In any case, we will have to wait until the start of next week to have better clarity on all of that.

In the meantime, just remember that you are not obliged to chase every move on your screen. The next two days could offer some trading opportunities but they could just as easily serve up a few nasty traps. So, be careful out there.

At times, following the market in enjoying a little time off isn't such a bad idea. As mentioned earlier this week, there will always be another opportunity to make money in markets. And you don't have to rush in to try and pick the bottom to do that.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: My Nvidia stock analysis shows bulls are better than what most seem to think
item.description:
Nvidia stock is rebuilding its bullish case. Can buyers get back above $155?

Nvidia has broken out of its recent descending channel, reclaimed two important trading areas and outperformed Nasdaq futures during its latest recovery. The next test is whether buyers can make those gains stick.

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) is giving bulls a few more reasons to stay constructive heading into the Thanksgiving holiday.

After falling to $141.17 on Wednesday, Nvidia recovered to $151.22 by the end of after-hours trading, a rebound of approximately 7.1% from the day's low. The stock had closed the regular session at $149.30, down 3.91%.

The recovery is also starting to make more sense from a technical perspective.

Three things Nvidia bulls have achieved

Looking at my hourly Nvidia chart, there are three encouraging developments, numbered accordingly.

1. Back inside the earnings value area

A value area is a price range in which a substantial proportion of trading volume took place during a selected period.

When a stock falls below its earnings-related value area, it suggests that the market is exploring lower prices. Returning inside that area is an early indication that the rejection of those previously accepted prices may be losing strength.

Nvidia has now achieved that.

2. Breaking out of the descending channel

Nvidia has escaped the blue descending channel on the chart and returned to its previous value area.

The combination is more encouraging than a channel breakout alone. Buyers have managed to interrupt the recent downward price structure while reclaiming territory where substantial trading previously occurred.

3. Approaching the earnings point of control

The point of control (PoC), represented by the red horizontal line, is the price at which the greatest trading volume occurred within the period being analyzed.

Think of it as a historical center of trading activity. It can attract price and become an area of contention between buyers and sellers.

Nvidia is approaching that area, around $153. Sustaining prices above it would represent another achievement for the bulls.

Nvidia is also showing some relative strength

Between 3 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET on November 25, Nvidia gained approximately 2.29%, compared with 0.74% for Nasdaq-100 futures.

That is an outperformance of 1.55 percentage points.

Admittedly, part of that recovery occurred outside regular trading hours. Still, Nvidia's ability to outperform the broader technology market during this particular window adds some credibility to the rebound.

As investingLive's Greg Michalowski noted in his latest Nasdaq technical analysis, both the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq-100 recovered sharply after testing support on Wednesday.

Four Nvidia stock price areas I am watching

  • $152.25 to $152.50: Immediate resistance. Sustaining prices above this area would strengthen the recovery case and bring the earnings PoC into play.

  • $155 to $155.50: The bigger test, incorporating Nvidia's November 17 closing price of $155.46, just before its earnings reaction. Reclaiming this area could change the broader technical picture.

  • $149 to $150.60: The first potential support area should Nvidia experience another pullback.

  • $147.50 to $147.75: A deeper area where buyers may attempt to regain control. Actual buying strength would need to emerge there.

A rejection near $152.50 followed by a failure to defend the first support area would weaken my bullish assessment.

Conversely, a break above resistance followed by a successful retest would be a healthy development.

Could bearish market positioning work in Nvidia's favor?

There are some interesting developments beyond the Nvidia chart.

Goldman Sachs reports that hedge funds have aggressively increased their short exposure, with a rise of approximately 19 percentage points in ETF shorts in a single week.

If equity prices stabilize, some of those traders may need to buy back their short positions, potentially accelerating a recovery.

Meanwhile, Citi points to extreme investor fear, noting that the S&P 500 was higher six months later in 13 of the previous 14 instances when the VIX reached 40.

Neither observation guarantees a market bottom, nor does the broader positioning data establish that Nvidia itself is heavily shorted. But both offer some perspective on the potential for a recovery.

AI investment continues, despite legitimate concerns about Nvidia

Australia's latest economic figures offer another interesting piece of the puzzle. Business investment surged 12.2% in the third quarter, with data centers and technology investment playing a prominent role.

And for a perspective on what this computing infrastructure could eventually enable, read Adam Button's thought-provoking piece on AI and recent developments in mathematics.

The technological opportunity remains considerable. Whether that opportunity translates into sufficient financial returns to justify current AI investments and stock valuations is a different question.

Nvidia also faces company-specific risks. S&P has placed Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, while Moody's has maintained its rating. Governance, management oversight and dependence on Jensen Huang remain legitimate investor concerns.

What Nvidia shareholders might consider

Investors uncomfortable with their exposure do not necessarily need to make an all-or-nothing decision.

Reducing part of an oversized position near resistance is one possibility. Another is maintaining exposure while monitoring whether Nvidia can establish support at higher prices.

Active traders considering selling some shares with the intention of buying them back at lower prices should also be prepared for the possibility that their desired pullback never arrives.

My Nvidia stock outlook

investingLive Tactical Recovery Score: +5/10 (moderately bullish)

This is my subjective directional assessment for the next one to three trading sessions, not a statistical probability of further gains.

For now, the bulls are doing fine. They have reclaimed two areas of value, escaped a descending channel and are approaching the earnings point of control.

They haven't repaired the entire post-earnings decline, but they are making progress.

With US stock exchanges closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and reopening for a shortened session on Friday, November 27, I would also allow for potentially thinner liquidity before drawing stronger conclusions from the next price move.

Analysis as of November 25, 2026, 8 p.m. ET. Trade at your own risk.

This article was written by Itai Levitan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Ray Dalio's 10-15% gold call resurfaces as bullion tries to find its feet
item.description:
High-profile endorsements like Dalio's rarely move gold on their own, but they can support retail and wealth-management demand at a time when prices have fallen sharply and some investors are reassessing their allocations. The renewed coverage also coincides with Wednesday's reversal off a 14-month low, which may encourage dip-buyers already watching the $3,500 area. The bigger near-term drivers remain real yields, the dollar and Fed rate expectations, so the long-term case Dalio describes is unlikely to stop short-term swings. For crypto, his skepticism about bitcoin as a reserve asset adds to a debate that matters for long-term institutional demand.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold claws back $160 from a 14-month low, but one candle doesn't necessarily make a bottom
  • Gold bulls may have been waiting months for a chart like this

---

Ray Dalio isn't telling anyone when to buy gold, only how much to hold, and after this year's slide that distinction is getting a fresh hearing.

Summary:

  • Ray Dalio's comments on Nicole Lapin's Money Rehab podcast, aired around November 9, have been widely picked up over the past day or so
  • He recommends a 10% to 15% gold allocation as a permanent diversifier, regardless of market expectations
  • Dalio links the case to rising US debt, now above $40 trillion, which he likens to plaque building up in arteries
  • He prefers gold to crypto because central banks can hold gold, while crypto can be monitored and seized, though he holds some bitcoin
  • The coverage comes as gold rebounds from a 14-month low near $3,425, still about a third below its January record
  • Forecasts remain split, with Natixis warning of $3,340 and UBS targeting $5,000 by end-2027

Ray Dalio's case for keeping 10% to 15% of a portfolio in gold is getting a second wind. Comments the Bridgewater Associates founder made on Nicole Lapin's Money Rehab podcast earlier this month have been picked up widely across financial and crypto media over the past day or so, just as bullion tries to recover from its lowest level in more than a year.

The interview aired around November 9, and the view itself isn't new. Dalio has recommended the same range before, including in August. What has changed is the backdrop. Gold fell to around $3,425 an ounce on Wednesday, its weakest since September 2025, before rebounding to close near $3,590, and it remains roughly a third below its January record.

A permanent holding, not a trade

Dalio's argument is about portfolio construction rather than timing. He recommends that investors hold gold in a 10% to 15% range whether they expect good or bad times for markets, treating it as a permanent diversifier rather than a bet on direction.

His reasoning rests on debt. Dalio has compared rising US government debt, now more than $40 trillion, to plaque building up in arteries, warning that the country is very exposed to a financial "heart attack" as interest costs crowd out other spending. In that kind of environment, he argues, printing money doesn't create wealth but erodes the value of money, and that is where gold earns its place.

Gold over crypto

Asked about crypto, Dalio said he finds gold the more appealing diversifier. He does hold some bitcoin, less than his gold, and declined to say how much. His main objection is about who can own each asset. Central banks can hold gold themselves, while crypto holdings can be monitored and legally seized, which he sees as a barrier to bitcoin becoming a reserve asset. He also leaned on the old observation that gold is the one asset that doesn't depend on anyone else's promise.

Why it lands now

The renewed attention reflects a split in the gold debate. In the short term, the outlook is clouded by a Federal Reserve that is still raising rates, a strong dollar and signs that central bank buying is slowing, and Natixis has warned gold could fall to $3,340 by January. Over the longer term, banks such as UBS still see $5,000 by the end of 2027, citing the same themes Dalio highlights, including sovereign debt and reserve diversification.

Dalio's framework sits firmly on the long-term side. It offers no view on where gold goes next week, and it would have recommended the same allocation at January's record high as at Wednesday's low. For investors, that is the practical point. His case is about how much gold to own, not when to buy it, which makes it a useful anchor after a fall of this size but not a signal that the bottom is in. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
